entry.title: fusevm, the Bytecode VM Under stryke and zshrs
entry.summary: How fusevm structures its opcode set, routes every execution tier through one op-semantics function, and lets stryke and zshrs share one runtime.
entry.content:
fusevm is a language-agnostic bytecode VM written in Rust. Frontends compile their source to a single Op enum, build a Chunk, and hand it to VM::run(). The VM does not know which language produced the bytecode. The fusevm README lists zshrs and stryke first among the frontends that target it.

This post covers the op set, the execution tiers, and how the two frontends divide the shared machinery.

Building and running a chunk

The core API is three types: ChunkBuilder, VM, and Value. From the README:

use fusevm::{Op, ChunkBuilder, VM, VMResult, Value};

let mut b = ChunkBuilder::new();
b.emit(Op::LoadInt(40), 1);
b.emit(Op::LoadInt(2), 1);
b.emit(Op::Add, 1);

let mut vm = VM::new(b.build());
match vm.run() {
    VMResult::Ok(val) => println!("result: {}", val.to_str()),  // "42"
    VMResult::Error(e) => eprintln!("error: {}", e),
    VMResult::Halted => {}
}

Execution is stack-based, with slot-indexed fast paths for locals.

The op set

The README counts 237 opcodes across 22 sections in src/op.rs. Besides the usual stack, variable, arithmetic, comparison, and control-flow ops, the set has dedicated sections for shell, AWK, higher-order, and concurrency semantics:

SectionCountExamples
Shell ops29Exec, PipelineBegin, Redirect, Glob
AWK ops61AwkFieldGet, AwkPrint, AwkGensub
Higher-order5MapBlock, GrepBlock, SortBlock
Cooperative concurrency12Go, ChanMake, ChanSend, Select
Fused11AccumSumLoop, SlotIncLtIntJumpBack
Extension2Extended(u16, u8), ExtendedWide(u16, usize)

Fused superinstructions

A frontend compiler that recognizes a common sequence can emit one fused op in its place. AccumSumLoop(sum, i, limit) replaces the seven-op sequence GetSlot + GetSlot + Add + SetSlot + PreInc + NumLt + JumpIfFalse for a counted sum loop. SlotIncLtIntJumpBack collapses a loop backedge into one dispatch. Each fused op removes the dispatch cycles and stack traffic of the ops it replaces.

One function defines op semantics

fusevm has four ways to run a chunk: the interpreter, three JIT tiers, and an ahead-of-time compiler. All of them route through, or fall back to, VM::exec_op in src/vm.rs, which the source documents as "the single source of truth for op semantics."

TierEntryHow it runs an op
InterpreterVM::runCalls exec_op per op in a dispatch loop
Linear / Block / Tracing JITJitCompilerEmits Cranelift IR for the eligible int/float/slot subset; anything else bails or deopts to the interpreter
AOTaot::compile_objectOne Cranelift block per op; unspecialized ops call exec_op through an extern "C" shim

A new op is implemented once, in exec_op, and every tier inherits it. The JIT and AOT paths only specialize the scalar ops; string, array, hash, and host ops stay in the interpreter.

The JIT tiers

The JIT uses Cranelift 0.130 behind the jit feature flag and emits native x86-64 or aarch64. A chunk is served by one of three tiers:

TierTriggerCoverage
LinearFirst call, if eligibleStraight-line expression chunks
Block1 invocation (default)Whole-chunk CFG: loops, branches, fused backedges, globals
Tracing50 backedges through a loop headerRecorded hot path, type-specialized, deopts on guard miss

Both thresholds can be set per process with FUSEVM_JIT_BLOCK_THRESHOLD and FUSEVM_JIT_TRACE_THRESHOLD, or per thread through TraceJitConfig.

On a tracing guard miss, the VM rebuilds the value stack and any inlined call frames, then resumes exec_op at the deopt IP.

The jit-disk-cache feature persists compiled code to ~/.cache/fusevm-jit, so codegen is skipped across process restarts. The aot feature lowers a whole chunk to a relocatable object through cranelift-object and links it against the runtime into a standalone executable; each frontend's --build calls into it.

How stryke and zshrs share it

Both frontends emit the same Op enum, and each reaches language-specific behavior through a different extension path.

zshrs emits no extended ops. Shell semantics go through the ShellHost trait, which handles Glob, TildeExpand, CmdSubst, Redirect, pipelines, traps, and the other shell ops. zshrs supplies the real implementation; without one the VM uses stubs that keep the stack balanced. Builtins lower to CallBuiltin(id, argc) with IDs from shell_builtins.rs plus zshrs's own.

stryke reserves two disjoint blocks of Extended op IDs: one at 0x0000 (ext_ops in fusevm_bridge.rs) and one at 0x1000 (nops in fusevm_native.rs). The VM dispatches them through a handler the frontend registers with VM::set_extension_handler. Because each frontend owns its own ID space, the tables do not conflict.

stryke's adoption is partial. Its README describes fusevm_bridge.rs as a tier-0 JIT that sends string-bearing segments to fusevm's block JIT, while stryke's own block JIT handles pure-integer segments. The repo's migration checklist sets the goal of retiring stryke's own vm.rs and jit.rs, and reports 126 of 362 stryke Op variants with native fusevm lowering.

The two also share a process. stryke depends on zshrs as a library, so both must resolve to one fusevm version. stryke's Cargo.toml requires fusevm = "0.26.7", the same minor zshrs uses, and explains why: fusevm defines about 54 #[no_mangle] symbols, and two semver-incompatible copies in one dependency graph fail to link on duplicate symbols.

Install

cargo add fusevm --features jit   # with Cranelift JIT
cargo add fusevm                  # interpreter only

Source and benchmarks are in the fusevm repository.

entry.title: Parallel Expect Playbooks with stryke-fleet
entry.summary: stryke-fleet is a pure-stryke package that adds transcripted PTY sessions, declarative playbooks, a recipe corpus for interactive CLIs, and parallel multi-target fan-out on top of stryke's pty builtins and pmap.
entry.content:
What it is

stryke-fleet is parallel expect/PTY automation written as a pure-stryke package. It has no [ffi] table and no cdylib; the installed package is stryke.toml plus lib/*.stk.

The spawn/expect/send loop itself is in strykelang core: pty_spawn, pty_send, pty_read, pty_expect, pty_expect_table, pty_buffer, pty_alive, pty_eof, pty_close, and pty_interact are builtins, and pmap provides the thread pool. The README describes what core does not provide as policy: what a step is, what a failed run returns, what an ssh login chain looks like, and what shape a transcript has. That policy lives in this package so it can be versioned independently of the language.

The four layers

ModuleRole
Fleet::SessionPTY session that records every send, match, timeout, and close
Fleet::PlaybookDeclarative step lists run in order against one session
Fleet::RecipesStep-list generators for common interactive CLIs
Fleet::FanoutOne playbook, N targets, one PTY per target in parallel

Session

Fleet::Session::open wraps a pty_spawn handle in a hashref with a log. send, expect, branch, and close append events, so a failed run returns the full interaction log rather than leaving a stuck process. Additions over the raw builtins include:

  • send_secret, which transmits the text but logs ***
  • send_control, for Ctrl-C, Ctrl-D, and similar
  • expect_exact, which quotemetas its argument for a literal match
  • expect_any, which reports which of several prompts arrived
  • drain, which reads until the child goes idle
  • transcript_text, which dumps one EVENT<TAB>DATA line per event

Playbook

A playbook is an arrayref of step hashrefs. The step keys are:

  • expect, branches, and send (each step needs at least one of these)
  • send_matched, which sends the result of the matching branch
  • timeout, in seconds (default 30)
  • name
  • optional
  • retries and retry_send
  • delay

The first non-optional expect or branch that times out fails the run, and the error names the step. run returns +{ ok, cmd, steps_run, transcript }, plus failed_step and error on failure. dry_run renders the steps without spawning anything.

Recipes

Recipes return playbook arrayrefs and never spawn anything themselves. That makes them composable with @{...} splices and testable without a network. Fleet::Recipes::names lists 48 generators. They include:

  • ssh_login, sudo, su, doas
  • psql, mysql, mariadb, redis_cli, mongo
  • telnet_login, sftp, scp, rsync
  • passwd_change, docker_login, cisco_enable, yes_to_all
  • restic, borg, age, vault_login, cryptsetup, bw_unlock

Fanout

Fleet::Fanout::run validates the steps once, then calls pmap { Fleet::Playbook::run($_, $steps, $opts) } over the command list. Each target gets its own PTY on its own thread, and results come back in target order. batch caps concurrency at K targets at a time. ssh builds ssh [opts] [user@]HOST commands from a host list.

Post-processing functions:

  • partition, count, summarize, and all_ok for pass/fail totals
  • group_by_error, which buckets failures by error string
  • group_by_output, which buckets successes by output; its doc comment describes this as config-drift detection
  • grep_transcript, which answers "which hosts printed X"
  • retry_failed and retry_until, which re-run only the failures

Usage

A local playbook from examples/local_demo.stk. It needs no network:

use Fleet

val $r = Fleet::Playbook::run("sh", [
    +{ send   => "echo fleet-$$\n" },
    +{ expect => qr/fleet-\d+/, timeout => 10, name => "echo back" },
    +{ send   => "exit\n" },
])

p $r->{ok} ? "ok — " . $r->{steps_run} . " steps" : "failed: " . $r->{error}

The main use case is one login recipe run against many hosts. From examples/parallel_ssh.stk:

h([@hosts], [@steps], +{ ssh_opts => "-o BatchMode=no" })
val $part    = Fleet::Fanout::partition($results)

ssh_login opens with a branch table. It accepts a host-key (yes/no)? prompt, a password prompt, or a shell prompt directly, and it is marked optional. It then optionally answers a password and expects the shell prompt.

An installer driven by yes_to_all, from examples/installer_autopilot.stk:

CLI

For one-shot expect/send from the shell:

The README directs anything with branches, retries, or more than two steps to a playbook script.

Scope boundary

The README separates Fleet from stryke's cluster([...]) + pmap_on, which are persistent SSH worker pools for non-interactive remote compute. Fleet is for sessions that prompt back.

How it's built and tested

Install with s pkg install -g github.com/MenkeTechnologies/stryke-fleet, or s pkg install -g . from a checkout.

t/test_fleet.stk is headless-CI safe by contract. Every PTY assertion drives a local cat or sh, and recipes are tested as data. tests/repo-contract.sh fails the build if any test in t/ spawns ssh or calls Fanout::ssh. CI installs a prebuilt stryke release, runs stryke -c on every .stk file in lib/, bin/, t/, and examples/, installs the package, and runs s test t/.

The package is MIT-licensed.

entry.title: MCP Servers as Single Native Binaries with stryke-mcpd
entry.summary: stryke-mcpd is a pure-stryke package that adds validated tool specs, crash-isolated serving, a root-jailed stock tool pack, and client helpers on top of stryke's built-in MCP support.
entry.content:
What it is

stryke-mcpd is a package for writing MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers in stryke. The README states the target: write the server in a few lines, s build --release it, ship one binary, with no Node runtime or Python venv on the target machine.

The protocol itself is not in this package. mcp_server_start, mcp_connect, mcp_tools, mcp_call, mcp_close, and the tool fn / mcp_server "name" { ... } desugar are strykelang core builtins. stryke-mcpd is the policy layer on top. It has no [ffi] table and no cdylib; the installed package is stryke.toml plus lib/*.stk.

The README states the rule for what belongs in the package:

If a function in this library can be replaced with one builtin call, it's a bug.

The two rules it enforces

The package exists to enforce two rules that stdio MCP servers depend on:

  1. stdout belongs to the protocol. A stray print corrupts the JSON-RPC stream. Mcpd::Server::log_to sends diagnostics to a file, and tests/repo-contract.sh greps lib/ and fails CI if any line writes to stdout.
  2. A dying tool must not kill the server. Every run coderef is wrapped. A die inside a tool comes back to the client as an ERROR: ... text result, the failure is logged, and the server keeps serving.

The wrapper strips the at FILE line N. suffix so the client sees only the message.

A minimal server

From examples/calc_server.stk:

use Mcpd

Mcpd::Server::serve("calc", [
    Mcpd::Schema::tool("add", "Add two numbers",
        +{ a => "number", b => "number" },
        fn { val $args = shift; $args->{a} + $args->{b} }),

    Mcpd::Schema::tool("reverse_text", "Reverse a string",
        +{ text => "string" },
        fn { val $args = shift; join("", reverse split "", $args->{text}) }),

    Mcpd::Schema::tool("always_fails", "Demonstrates the error envelope",
        +{},
        fn { die "intentional failure" }),
])

serve validates and wraps every spec, then hands the set to mcp_server_start. It blocks for the life of the server.

Round trip from the client side

From examples/round_trip.stk, which connects to the server above over stdio:

Wiring into an MCP client config is { "command": "stryke", "args": ["server.stk"] }, or a built binary with no args.

The four modules

ModuleRole
Mcpd::SchemaConstruction-time spec validation, arg checking, JSON Schema conversion
Mcpd::Serverserve, error wrapping, arg-checked serving, file-only logging
Mcpd::ToolsStock tool pack, root-jailed
Mcpd::ClientResult-envelope extraction and call-then-extract helpers

Schema. mcp_server_start accepts any {name, description, parameters, run} hashref and reports errors one tool at a time when the server starts. Mcpd::Schema::tool does the checks at construction time instead: the name must be an identifier, the description must be non-empty, each parameter type must be one of string number boolean array object, and run must be a coderef. check_args rejects missing params, undeclared extras, and mistyped numbers, arrays, and objects. to_json_schema and to_tool_list render the MCP inputSchema and tools/list payloads. from_json_schema and from_tool_list convert them back.

Server. Besides serve and wrap, checked and wrap_all_checked run check_args before the body, so a malformed call becomes an ERROR: envelope before the tool body runs.

Tools. Mcpd::Tools::all returns the stock pack: filesystem read, list, glob, grep, find, stat, du, head, tail, slice, hash, write, append, replace, chmod, mkdir, touch, rmdir, delete, copy, and move, plus sh_exec, env_get, time_now, and sys_info. Every filesystem path goes through Mcpd::Tools::jail, which normalizes ., .., and // lexically. A path that resolves outside the root dies, and the server wrapper turns that into an error result. all(+{ readonly => 1 }) leaves out the mutating tools (fs_write through fs_move, and sh_exec). sh_exec takes an allow arrayref of permitted command words. Without allow, it runs any command.

From examples/jailed_fs.stk, an escape attempt over a live connection:

Client. text, texts, text_lines, content_of_type, is_error, error_message, tool_names, tool_schema, and the call_text / call_lines / call_texts composites unpack the +{content => [+{type => "text", text => ...}]} envelope.

CLI

How it's built and tested

Install with s pkg install -g github.com/MenkeTechnologies/stryke-mcpd, or s pkg install -g . from a checkout. No cargo step is involved.

t/test_mcpd.stk tests Schema, Tools, and Client as pure functions, then runs a live round trip. It generates a server script, connects over stdio, lists and calls tools, calls one that dies, and confirms the next call on the same connection still succeeds. The CI job installs a prebuilt stryke release tarball, runs stryke -c on every .stk file in lib/, bin/, t/, and examples/, installs the package, and runs s test t/. Separate jobs run the shell gates under tests/, including the stdout check.

entry.title: Pipelines, Threading, and Parallel Primitives in stryke
entry.summary: How stryke combines Perl 5 syntax with pipe-forward, a threading macro, and rayon-backed parallel builtins.
entry.content:
stryke is a dynamic language implemented in Rust. The README describes it as an interpreter that "parses and executes Perl 5 scripts with rayon-powered work-stealing primitives across every CPU core." On top of the Perl 5 base it adds pipe-forward, a threading macro, implicit block parameters, and a family of parallel builtins. A --compat flag turns all of those extensions off for running unmodified Perl.

This post covers the pipeline syntax and the parallel primitives. Every example below was run against stryke v0.17.60 with stryke -e.

Execution model

The README's architecture section lays out the pipeline: lexer, recursive-descent and Pratt parser, compiler to bytecode, then a match-dispatch VM with a Cranelift block JIT. Hot subs are handed to the JIT after a configurable number of VM invocations (STRYKE_JIT_SUB_INVOKES, default 50), and --no-jit disables it. Values are a NaN-boxed u64 (StrykeValue) that holds immediates inline and points at Arc<HeapObject> for strings, arrays, hashes, and the rest.

Warm starts skip lex, parse, and compile by reading from an rkyv shard at ~/.stryke/scripts.rkyv, which is mmapped for zero-copy lookup.

String-bearing code segments are lowered to fusevm, the bytecode VM stryke shares with zshrs. Moving all execution onto fusevm is in progress; the migration checklist in the repo reports 126 of 362 stryke Op variants lowered.

Pipe-forward: |>

|> is desugared at parse time. It passes the left side as the first argument of the call on the right, and associates left. map, grep/filter, sort, and e accept a blockless expression on the right-hand side:

1..5 |> map $_ * $_ |> join "," |> p
# 1,4,9,16,25

Per the README, |> binds looser than || and tighter than ?: and and/or/not, so $x + 1 |> f parses as f($x + 1).

The threading macro: ~>

~> (aliases thread, t, ->>) chains stages without repeating |>. Stages can be bare function names, functions that take a block, parenthesized calls with _ as the placeholder, or anonymous blocks written >{ }. Inside blocks, bare _ is the topic ($_), and _1 is the second positional.

Block-taking stages chain directly, and |> ends the macro:

} sort{$_1 <=> $_0} |> join "," |> p
# 400,324,256,196,144,100,64,36,16,4

Anonymous blocks and placeholder calls:

The README's guidance: use ~> when most stages take blocks, and |> for blockless expressions and unary functions.

Parallel primitives

Every parallel builtin runs on rayon's work-stealing pool. The README states that each parallel block runs in its own interpreter context with captured lexical scope, and -j N sets the thread count. The parallel forms slot into pipelines like the sequential ones:

 = @data |> psort { _ <=> _1 }; p join ",", @s
# 1,3,5,9

val @n = 1..100; val $s = @n |> preduce { _ + _1 }; p $s
# 5050

pmap_reduce fuses the map and the reduction:

fan_cap N { ... } runs a block N times in parallel with the index as the topic and returns results in index order:

Streaming

pmaps, pgreps, and pflat_maps are lazy. The README describes them as bounded-memory iterators that emit output as it completes, so an unbounded source can be cut off with take:

Pipeline objects

par_pipeline builds a rayon-backed chain; par_pipeline_stream runs stages concurrently over bounded crossbeam channels and, per the README, does not preserve order. In v0.17.60 the method-call form works for both:

 <=> $b } @r
# 1992,1994,1996,1998,2000

Shared state: varsync

Workers get a copy of captured lexicals by default. A plain my counter incremented inside pfor is unchanged when the loop finishes:

To share state you opt in with varsync, which wraps the variable in Arc<Mutex>. Compound operators (++, +=, .=, |=, &=) hold the lock for the whole read-modify-write:

Further reading

The strykelang README also covers channels (pchannel, pselect), barrier, ploop/pwhile, ppool, the parallel file-IO builtins (par_lines, par_walk, glob_par), and pmap_on for spreading a map across an SSH worker pool. stryke docs pmap opens the built-in reference at that topic.

entry.title: stryke web — A Rails-Shaped Framework for stryke
entry.summary: What the stryke web generator and runtime ship today, and which parts of the design doc are still targets.
entry.content:
stryke web is the web framework for strykelang. It has two halves: a Rust CLI, s_web, that generates .stk source for a new app, and a set of web_* runtime builtins inside the stryke interpreter that serve it. The design doc is docs/WEB_FRAMEWORK.md; the generator reference is stryke_web/README.md.

The design doc marks its own status: Phase 0 shipped, most of Phase 1 shipped, Phase 2 mostly deferred, Phase 3 not started. This post follows that split.

Architecture

LayerLanguageLocation
Generator CLI (s_web new, g, s, db, routes)Ruststryke_web/
Generated app code (config/routes.stk, controllers, models)strykethe user's app directory
Framework runtime (web_route, web_render, ORM, migrations)Rust builtinsstrykelang/web.rs, strykelang/web_orm.rs

The stryke_web crate opts out of the parent workspace with its own [workspace] table, so it builds independently of the interpreter. Its only runtime dependencies are clap and heck.

Shipped: the generator

s_web new myblog
cd myblog
s_web g scaffold Post title:string body:text published:bool
# routes.stk — add `web_resources "posts"`
s_web db migrate
bin/server
# open http://localhost:3000/posts

s_web g scaffold writes a model, a migration, a 7-action controller, and 5 ERB views. The generated controller calls model class methods that delegate to the web_model_* builtins:

Other generators: controller, model, migration, app PRESET, auth, admin, api, mailer, job, channel, docker, ci, pwa. s_web new also takes flags that run several of these at once:

Presets include blog, ecommerce, saas, cms, forum, crm, helpdesk and others. Themes include simple, dark, pico, bootstrap, tailwind, and four CSS-only neon themes (cyberpunk, synthwave, terminal, matrix). --docker, --ci, and --pwa add a multi-stage Dockerfile, a GitHub Actions workflow that runs migrate + boot + a /health smoke check, and a PWA manifest plus service worker.

Shipped: the runtime

Routing is a set of builtins called from config/routes.stk:

The runtime surface, grouped:

  • Request/response: web_params, web_request, web_render (html/text/json/template), web_redirect, web_set_header, web_status. An action that calls neither web_render nor web_redirect renders app/views/{resource}/{action}.html.erb.
  • Templates: ERB with <%= %>, <% %>, <%# %>, <%- -%>, layouts, and web_render_partial. Control structures can span tags because the engine compiles all segments into one stryke program before running it.
  • Data: SQLite by default (web_db_connect, web_db_query, web_db_execute), the web_model_* CRUD set, pagination, LIKE search, soft delete, counter caches, single-IN-query eager loading (web_model_with), and transactions.
  • Migrations: web_create_table, web_add_column, web_remove_column, web_drop_table, web_migrate/web_rollback, tracked in schema_migrations.
  • Jobs: database-backed queue (web_jobs_init, web_job_enqueue/dequeue/complete/fail).
  • Security and auth: CSRF meta tag, web_security_headers, web_permit strong params, cookie sessions and flash, JWT (HS256), TOTP, token-bucket rate limiting, signed time-limited tokens, web_can.
  • APIs: /openapi.json, Swagger UI at /docs, and Redoc at /docs/redoc are served from the live route table with no app code. JSON:API envelope helpers and web_bearer_token are included.
  • Streaming: SSE via web_sse_event and web_render_stream.

s_web build generates a Rust wrapper crate that embeds every .stk file with include_str!; cargo build --release inside it produces one binary containing the framework, the app, and statically linked SQLite. The README reports one such build at 136 MB on macOS arm64.

Shipped behavior that differs from the design doc

Some shipped pieces are simpler than the doc's target form:

AreaDesign doc targetShipped
Template outputoriginally #{ expr }, compiled AOT via CraneliftERB <%= %>, compiled to a stryke program at request time
Routing DSLroute :GET, "/", home#index, resources :postsweb_route / web_resources / web_root builtins
Password storageArgon2idSHA-256 + salt (web_password_hash)
JSONsimd-jsonserde_json
ORMjoins, scopes, callbackssingle-table chains; joins/scopes pending

The template change is recorded in the doc's Resolved Decisions (2026-05-01): ERB replaced #{} for visual parity with Rails.

Not shipped yet

From the doc's phase list, deferred or not started:

  • HTTP/2 via h2 and TLS via rustls.
  • WebSockets and the Channel abstraction (generators scaffold channel stubs only).
  • glommio + io_uring thread-per-core runtime, per-core sharding.
  • Mailer runtime (SMTP); the generator writes the structure.
  • Polished hot reload, TechEmpower harness, public benchmark dashboard.
  • Phase 3: HTTP/3 default-on, kTLS, custom SIMD HTTP parser, wasm32-wasi edge target.

s_web console is marked pending a stryke --repl flag.

Performance: targets, not measurements

The design doc has a performance table: 500k req/s plaintext for Phase 0, rising to 6M+ for Phase 3, plus cold-start and memory targets. These are design targets. For Phase 0 the doc says the number is "still subject to TechEmpower-style validation", and the Phase 1 targets are "pending Phase 2 perf work." No TechEmpower results are published in the repo. Local benchmarks run through s bench.

The one wall-clock figure in the generator README is about scaffolding, not serving: about 0.45 s to generate and migrate the everything preset.

Source: docs/WEB_FRAMEWORK.md, stryke_web/README.md, and strykelang/web.rs in strykelang.

entry.title: zpwr, a Terminal Environment Behind One Verb Dispatcher
entry.summary: How zpwr installs, where its files live, and how its single dispatcher command exposes diagnostics, profiling, and snapshot tooling.
entry.content:
zpwr is a terminal environment built on zinit. It configures the shell, tmux (ztmux), vim, completion and keybindings from a single repository. The README credits Hashrocket's Dotmatrix as the original fork point. The installer sets zshrs as the login shell; stock zsh remains supported.

Most of the environment is reached through one command: zpwr <verb>.

Installing

One line:

sh -c "$(curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/MenkeTechnologies/zpwr/main/install/s)"

install/s is a wrapper around the manual path:

.zpwr/install && ./zpwrInstall.sh

The installer confirms what it will install and overwrite before it runs. It builds the Rust toolchain components with cargo in the background, adds zshrs to /etc/shells and runs chsh. If zshrs is not on PATH when cargo finishes, it falls back to stock zsh. Zinit installs plugins on the first shell after install.

zpwrInstall.sh takes these flags:

FlagEffect
-aInstall all dependencies
-cCopy just configs
-nDo not start ztmux at end of installer
-sSkip main section
-hDisplay help
-VDisplay script version

-c is the minimal install: configs only, no dependencies. The scripts in ~/.zpwr/install can then be run one at a time.

Layout

Everything lives under ~/.zpwr (the ZPWR variable). ~/.zshrc, ~/.vimrc, ~/.tmux.conf and the other configs are symlinked into $HOME. Previous configs are archived under ~/.zpwr/local.

Top-level directories at origin/main:

PathContents
autoload/autoloaded functions, split by common, darwin, linux, fzf, comps, comp_utils, systemctl
env/environment and the verb table (env/zpwr.zsh)
install/installer scripts
scripts/standalone scripts
tests/zunit test files
man/man1/zpwr.1, zpwrall.1
tmux/tmux configuration
local/per-user state, git ignored

Two files carry user customization and survive zpwr update:

  • ~/.zpwr/local/.tokens.sh, sourced before zsh config and zinit startup
  • ~/.zpwr/local/.tokens-post.sh, sourced after all of it

Extra zinit plugins go in the post file:

The dispatcher

env/zpwr.zsh builds a global associative array, ZPWR_VERBS. Each key is a verb; each value is function=description:

 time with percentiles and baseline diff'

zpwr sources that file with the caller's arguments on every call. zpwr <tab> gives grouped menu completion over the same table. zpwr verbs lists verbs in arb and runs the ones you pick, and zpwr verbsedit puts them on the command line.

Counts from the table at origin/main:

^]]+)\]=/' | sort -u | wc -l
# 460
git show origin/main:env/zpwr.zsh | perl -ne "print \"\$1\n\" if /^\s*ZPWR_VERBS\[[^]]+\]='([^=]+)=/" | sort -u | wc -l
# 373

That is 460 distinct verb names mapped onto 373 backing functions. Several verbs are aliases of each other; wizard and docs both run zpwrWizard. The README also lists 2000+ aliases and 360+ git aliases.

Selected verbs

zpwr doctor

Scans for stale .zwc files, zcompdump freshness, duplicate and missing PATH/FPATH entries, broken symlinks, invalid named directories, missing dependencies, zinit installation, history files and config symlinks. Output is pass/warn/fail per check, then a summary.

zpwr bench / zpwr startup / zpwr flame

Three views of startup cost:

bench stores its baseline and history in $ZPWR_LOCAL/zpwr-bench-baseline.txt and $ZPWR_LOCAL/zpwr-bench-history.txt.

zpwr snapshot / zpwr restore

zpwr snapshot [name] writes named directories, aliases, environment variables, history, the directory stack, git repo status, tmux layout and vim sessions to $ZPWR_LOCAL/snapshots/. Restore can be partial:

Components are hash, aliases, env, tmux, vim, history, dirs. History is merged, not overwritten.

zpwr pathaudit / zpwr lint / zpwr ports

  • pathaudit checks PATH, FPATH and MANPATH for duplicates, missing directories and world-writable directories.
  • lint runs zsh -n on autoloads and env files and shellcheck on scripts/ and install/.
  • ports lists listening TCP ports with process, PID, user and bind address; -k PORT kills the owner.

Under zshrs

zshrs implements syntax highlighting, autosuggestions, autopair and history substring search in the shell itself, and ships a native powerlevel10k prompt engine. When $ZSHRS_VERSION is set, zpwr sets ZPWR_NATIVE_ZLE=true and skips the four equivalent zsh plugins so widgets are not wrapped twice. zshrs also adds an async_precmd hook that runs after the prompt is drawn. zpwr moves only the hooks named in ZPWR_PRECMD_ASYNC_HOOKS there, and the default list is zpwrPrecmd.

Tests, docs, removal

  • zpwr test runs the zunit suite; zpwr testall includes plugin tests. origin/main has 149 tests/*.zsh files.
  • man zpwr is the quick reference and man zpwrall is the full verb and variable catalog. Add $ZPWR/man to MANPATH first.
  • zpwr updateall relinks configs, pulls, updates plugins, regenerates caches and updates dependencies.
  • zpwr uninstall asks for confirmation, restores backups, unlinks configs and deletes the config directories.

entry.title: zsh-more-completions, Layout, Install and How Completions Get In
entry.summary: How the zsh-more-completions corpus is split across directories, how its plugin file wires them into fpath, and how new completion files are harvested and checked.
entry.content:
zsh-more-completions is a zsh plugin made of #compdef completion files for compsys. The README says most files were first generated from --help output, man pages and web research, then cleaned and updated by hand, and that many were written by hand from the start.

The README also treats the corpus as reference material. Each _command file uses the same schema: a #compdef header, then _arguments / _describe blocks that list subcommands, flags and arguments with descriptions. You can read a command's options from its file without installing the command.

Size

All counts below come from origin/main at c66e5683dd. The repo has a stats script, scripts/print-repo-stats.zsh, that counts _* files with find -maxdepth 1 -type f in each completion directory. This tree query counts the same files without a checkout:

git ls-tree -r --name-only origin/main \
  | perl -ne 'print "$1\n" if m{^([^/]+)/_[^/]*$}' | sort | uniq -c
Directory_* filesPurpose (README)
src/8,360main completions
more_src/13,128additional (0-9, a-c)
more_src2/4,497additional (d-g)
more_src3/3,788additional (h-l)
more_src4/5,244additional (m-p)
more_src5/3,717additional (q-s)
more_src6/3,973additional (t-z)
more_src7/100automated generation
more_src8/100automated generation
man_src/3,398parsed from man pages
override_src/22overrides, prepended to fpath
architecture_src/1,067cross-architecture toolchains
total47,394

The README headline says 47,398. It also says counts change constantly and should never be edited by hand, and points to the stats script for live numbers.

architecture_src/ holds target-prefixed toolchain binaries such as _aarch64-alpine-linux-musl-gcc. override_src/ is a short list (_git, _curl, _whois, _ztmux, _zshrs and others) meant to win over completions found elsewhere on fpath.

How the plugin loads

zsh-more-completions.plugin.zsh is 18 lines. It does not autoload anything and does not call compinit. It only edits fpath:

 ... "$1/man_src" "$1/architecture_src")

override_src is prepended. Every other directory is appended, after the system completion directories, so a completion shipped with zsh or the OS still wins over the plugin's copy. Each directory is added only if it is not already on fpath.

Installing

Zinit (README: recommended)

nocompletions stops zinit from symlinking every file into ~/.zinit/completions. The plugin's own fpath ordering then applies, so override_src stays first and system completions stay ahead of the rest.

Oh My Zsh

Add zsh-more-completions to plugins. OMZ adds only the plugin root to fpath, so the README gives a loop to run before OMZ calls compinit. It adds each *src directory, putting override directories first:

   if [[ -d "$dir" ]]; then
                if [[ -z ${fpath[(r)$dir]} ]];then
                    if [[ $dir = *override* ]]; then
                        fpath=($dir $fpath)
                    else
                        fpath=($fpath $dir)
                    fi
                fi
            fi
        done
    fi
done

A comment in the plugin file says that under OMZ, compinit has to run twice: once in OMZ, and once after the plugin file is sourced.

Manual

Clone the repo and copy the _* files from the source directories to a directory on your fpath.

Then

The README suggests compinit -C for faster startup. It skips the security check and loads the cached ~/.zcompdump.

How completions are added

The scripts/ directory holds the harvesters:

  • harvest-apt-completions.py
  • harvest-brew-completions.py
  • harvest-crates-completions.py
  • harvest-gh-releases.py
  • harvest-nix-completions.py
  • harvest-web-completions.py

The Homebrew harvester's docstring gives the pipeline for each formula:

  1. Skip if _<formula> is already in src/ or more_src/, or is in blacklist.txt.
  2. Run brew fetch --quiet <formula> to pull the bottle without installing it.
  3. Stream-extract share/zsh/site-functions/_* from the tarball.
  4. Dedup, validate with zsh -nf, write headers and body to more_src/_<stem>, and add the stem to the blacklist.

blacklist.txt (51,623 lines at this commit) is the dedup ledger. Once a command name is covered, harvesters skip it. The APT harvester loads and merges the same file.

The README's harvest list goes past package managers: Nix, Homebrew, APT, Fedora, Alpine, FreeBSD, Kali, crates.io, npm, and source-level work on scientific and infrastructure toolkits. For many of those, it says flag tables were read from each tool's usage() function, argparse setup or man page source.

Hand-written files follow the same rules. The files in override_src/ show the format, for example _whois:

Tests

GitHub Actions runs the same command on Ubuntu. At this commit, tests/ has 22 .zsh files with 22,642 @test entries (git grep -h '^@test' origin/main -- 'tests/*.zsh' | wc -l). Among the checks:

  • every override_src file starts with #compdef, and every src file starts with #compdef or #autoload (t-headers.zsh)
  • conventions such as _files for filename arguments, bracketed option descriptions, and combined short and long option specs (t-conventions.zsh)
  • blacklist.txt exists, is non-empty and has no duplicate lines, and the CI workflow contract holds (t-repo-invariants.zsh)

entry.title: Inside zshrs - A zsh Port in Rust Split Into Ported Code and Extensions
entry.summary: How zshrs is laid out — a mechanically enforced 1:1 port of zsh's C source, a separate extensions tree, and a fusevm bytecode core underneath both.
entry.content:
zshrs is a drop-in zsh replacement written in Rust. Every command — interactive, script, function, sourced file — is compiled to fusevm bytecode rather than walked as an AST, and compiled chunks are persisted across processes in rkyv images.

This post covers the layout of the codebase and the rules that keep it honest. A follow-up covers the compile pipeline and cache.

Workspace

The repository is a 4-crate workspace:

CrateRole
zshrsThe runtime
zshrs-daemonIPC, HTTP, fsnotify, cache maintenance
znativePublished SDK for native Rust plugins
zshrs-runtimeEmits libzsh.a for AOT linking, kept separate so cargo install zshrs does not build it

Shipped binaries live in bins/: zshrs (always built), zshrs-recorder (--features recorder) and zd (--features zd).

Ported code vs extensions

The runtime source is divided into directories with different rules:

DirectoryRule
src/ported/Strict 1:1 port. Every .rs mirrors a real upstream Src/<x>.c; every top-level fn carries /// Port of <cname>() from Src/<file>.c:NNNN; no invented helpers; file set frozen.
src/compsys/ported/1:1 mirror of zsh's Completion/ tree. Engine functions are ported to Rust; end-user completers are copied as-is and dispatched through a _call_function bridge.
src/extensions/Features zsh C does not have. Must not duplicate or shadow a port.
src/recorder/Feature-gated; every symbol is #[cfg(feature = "recorder")].

The boundary is enforced by a test, tests/port_purity.rs, not by convention. The lexer and parser are direct ports of Src/lex.c and Src/parse.c, and zsh's AST shape (ZshProgram → ZshList → ZshSublist → ZshPipe → ZshCommand) is kept as-is. The bytecode compiler, ZshCompiler, is the original Rust part.

Things that live in src/extensions/ include AOT, plugin/script/autoload caches, the worker pool, ZWC helpers, and native line-editor engines ported from fish (syntax highlighting, autosuggestions, history search, autopair).

No tree walker

The tree-walking interpreter has been removed, and tests keep it removed. tests/tree_walker_absent.rs asserts that the old recursive dispatch functions (execute_simple, execute_pipeline, execute_list, execute_compound, execute_command_bg) do not exist in the source, and that execute_command goes through the parser and ZshCompiler. tests/no_tree_walker_dispatch.rs pins the behavior of every construct the deleted walker used to handle.

In-process execution

zshrs replaces many fork + exec paths with in-process work. From the README's comparison table:

Operationzshzshrs
$(cmd)fork + pipeIn-process stdout capture via dup2
cat, head, sort, wc, …fork + execBuiltin
**/*.rsSingle-threaded opendirParallel per-subdir descent on a rayon pool
compinitSynchronous fpath scanBackground scan on the worker pool
AutoloadRead + parse every timeBytecode loaded from rkyv

48 coreutils commands are builtins — the entries of EXT_BUILTIN_NAMES in src/extensions/ext_builtins.rs that GNU coreutils also installs.

The worker pool is configured in ~/.zshrs/zshrs.toml:

[worker_pool]
size = 8

[glob]
parallel_threshold = 32
recursive_parallel = true

Extensions built on the pool include async/await, pmap, pgrep, peach and barrier, plus an intercept builtin for before/after/around advice on any command word:

intercept after '_*' { echo "$INTERCEPT_NAME took ${INTERCEPT_MS}ms" }

The { … } body form is a zshrs syntax extension; zshrs --zsh turns it off and rejects it the way /bin/zsh does.

Compatibility checks

The project measures compatibility against reference shells rather than manuals:

  • tests/emulation_parity.rs compares stdout and exit status of zshrs --X against the real shell X for the Bourne-family drop-ins (--zsh, --bash, --ksh, --mksh, --pdksh, --sh/--posix, --dash, --ash).
  • bins/parity-fuzz.rs runs grammar-driven, seed-replayable snippets through both zshrs and zsh and flags divergences.
  • tests/ztst_runner.rs runs upstream zsh's own .ztst files.

The README reports test counts measured on 2026-10-27:

SuiteTests
parity49,500
zsh_construct_corpus396
no_tree_walker_dispatch174
zsh_corpus_via_new_pipeline123
zsh_parser_probe87
compile_zsh_smoke29
tree_walker_absent8

Performance as reported

The README publishes hyperfine results (release build 0.13.27, Darwin arm64) and they are mixed. A few rows, mean milliseconds:

Workloadzshrszsh
Startup (no-op)7.44.6
Arithmetic loop (100000)178.4122.3
String append (5000)23.852.4
Command substitution (500)90.3268.9
External spawn (200)226.1315.4

zshrs is ahead on command substitution, string append and external spawn, and behind on no-op startup, arithmetic loops and function calls in this run. The full table and the harness are in bench/.

Install

stall zshrs

Source and docs: github.com/MenkeTechnologies/zshrs.

entry.title: How zshrs Compiles Shell Code and Caches It in rkyv
entry.summary: The zshrs pipeline from zsh source to fusevm bytecode, its tiered JIT, and the rkyv cache that lets later processes skip lexing, parsing and compiling.
entry.content:
zshrs does not interpret an AST. Every command is lexed and parsed by ports of zsh's C front end, compiled to fusevm bytecode, and run on a VM. Compiled chunks are persisted in rkyv files, so a script or autoload function compiled by one process can be loaded by the next without going through the front end again.

The pipeline

From the README:

Interactive command  ──► lex::zshlex ──► parse::parse ──► ZshCompiler ──► fusevm::Op ──► VM::run()
Script file (first)  ──► lex::zshlex ──► parse::parse ──► ZshCompiler ──► VM::run() ──► persist rkyv shard
Script file (cached) ──► index.rkyv + mmap shard ──► deserialize Chunk ──► VM::run()
Autoload function    ──► autoloads.rkyv ──► deserialize Chunk ──► VM::run()

lex::zshlex and parse::parse are ports of Src/lex.c and Src/parse.c. ZshCompiler is the only original piece of the front end. It targets the same Op enum that strykelang uses, so both languages share fused superinstructions, extension dispatch and the Cranelift JIT path.

Execution tiers

Inside fusevm::VM::run() a chunk lands on one of several tiers:

TierWhatWhen
rkyv image hitSkip lex/parse/compileWarm script runs
Block JITNative code via CraneliftLoops, conditionals
Linear JITNative code via CraneliftStraight-line arithmetic
InterpreterJump table + superinstructionsBuiltins, I/O, strings

Enabling the JIT does not mean a given chunk is JIT-compiled. zshrs --tiers runs a script and then asks fusevm which tier took each chunk, using fusevm's own predicates (is_block_eligible, block_jit_is_compiled, trace_is_compiled, find_jit_region). For chunks that reached neither JIT tier it lists the op kinds responsible:

zshrs --tiers script.zsh

Cache layout

Everything lives under $ZSHRS_HOME (default ~/.zshrs/):

PathContents
index.rkyvIndex: fq_name → shard id, generation, byte offset
images/{hash8}-*.rkyvMmap-ready shards (system, completions, plugins, scripts, .zshrc, …)
autoloads.rkyvOne compiled program per autoloaded function
scripts.rkyvOne chunk per script run; per-event chunks for sourced files
deparse.rkyvDeparsed function bodies (what $functions prints)

The SQLite files in the same directory — catalog.db and the views used by dbview — are read-only mirrors for inspection. The README states they are never consulted for cache hit/miss or execution. history.db and zshrs_history.db hold history and are unrelated to bytecode caching.

Invalidation keys

Each store keys its entries on what determines the compiled output:

  • Autoloads: function name, the resolved fpath directory, a SHA-256 of the exact definition text, and the identity of the zshrs binary that compiled it. An edited function recompiles. Each entry also records what the $fpath search found, so a later load can skip the search while the directory is still on fpath and those files are unchanged.
  • Scripts: path, mtime, build, and the alias/option state the first run started from. A file that changes aliases or options itself is not stored.
  • Deparse: SHA-256 of the name, body text and the option state the body is re-lexed under, plus the binary identity.

The autoload cache is bypassed for ksh_autoload-style bodies and for autoload without -U, because there the compiled program is not a function of the file's bytes alone.

Measured effect

The README reports two sets of numbers.

For _git (424 KB of shell): the first git <tab> in a process goes from 1.06 s to 0.56 s once the chunk is cached; decoding the cached 4.6 MB chunk costs 229 µs versus 318 ms to parse and compile the file.

The README's cold vs warm comparison (it does not name the workload):

Cold (cache miss):  717ms  — lex + parse + compile + cache write + execute
Warm (cache hit):     7ms  — deserialize + execute

Prewarming

Autoload entries are written through on first call, one per function actually used. To compile a whole directory up front:

s            # every dir on $fpath
zshrs --prewarm-autoloads DIR ...    # just these
zd prewarm [DIR ...]                 # via the daemon
prewarm-autoloads [DIR ...]          # as a builtin inside a shell

Entries already current are skipped by SHA-256, so a re-run after adding one plugin compiles only the new completers. The README gives a sizing budget of roughly 6x the source size: a 13k-completer directory compiles to 165 MB in 35 s on a debug build. zshrs-recorder runs this pass at the end of every recording (--no-prewarm skips it); it must not run beside a live ZLE because the parser uses process-global lexer state.

Inspecting the cache

dbview reads the mirrors without SQL:

Source: github.com/MenkeTechnologies/zshrs.
